source.title: Inference-Time Vulnerability Beyond Shallow Safety: Alignment Along Generation Trajectories

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests whether injection vulnerability is confined to the opening tokens and reports that it can persist at later generation steps, while being strongest early and varying by model. It also tests trajectory-level training as a refinement intended to improve robustness.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure per-token KL divergence, fine-tune models on a few harmful or benign prompt-response examples, or test whether safety resides in a small set of weights. Its benign-phrase results concern inference-time token injection, not benign fine-tuning. Omitted table results include Table 1's non-AdvBench benchmark cells for injection and trajectory-alignment comparisons, Table 2's non-prefilling attacks and other benchmark cells, Table 9, Tables 3 and 12–17, and other figure-only trajectory analyses; the retained rows prioritize direct injection, training under injection, prefilling, and an explicit benign-phrase injection result.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful compliance when tokens are forced into the response at step 0 (prefilling) and at later steps, using direct ASR (V4). It argues that shallow safety is a special case of a vulnerability that persists past the opening tokens, more in some models than others. It also trains a recovery-style deepening defense and measures how well it holds up under injection, prefilling, suffix and PAIR attacks, plus its costs (V7). It does not test fine-tuning attacks, per-token KL or parameter localization.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that shallow (prefix) safety is a special case of a broader inference-time vulnerability. Short injections at any step can redirect generation, strongest early but persisting to a degree that varies by model. Refusal-like hidden states do not predict robustness. Iterative SimPO training on bidirectionally augmented trajectories drives injection ASR toward zero and transfers to prefilling, I-GCG and PAIR. The paraphrase omits that the authors themselves note Mistral's prefilling resistance is weak under the OM judge.
record.recipe_differences: This is not a reproduction of either original method. It studies arbitrary-step token injection and introduces iterative SimPO training on augmented generation trajectories; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or per-token KL measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Injection effects vary by model and generation step: the effect is strongest early; the paper reports Llama's harmful-injection effect no longer above baseline after about step 7, while Mistral maintains elevated ASR later and Qwen is nearly unaffected by refusal injections. Outcomes also vary by benchmark and judge. The paper uses greedy decoding only.

fits_no_version.finding: Harmful injections raise ASR, and refusal injections suppress it, at arbitrary generation steps. The effect is strongest early and persistence varies by model. Llama base ASR at fixed steps is 59/67 (step 0), 23/29 (step 5), 4/2 (step 10), 0/0 (step 20). Mistral stays elevated late, and Qwen stays high under harmful injection throughout.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vulnerability to forced tokens is not confined to the response opening; how far past the opening it persists varies by model.

fits_no_version.finding: Cosine similarity of pre-injection hidden states with a refusal prototype does not predict resistance to injection.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-like internal states do not confer robustness to trajectory perturbation.

record.problems: The reported evaluation uses greedy decoding only, and the authors identify extending evaluation to stochastic decoding as future work. The trajectory augmentation uses AdvBench and a single harmful injection sequence selected through ablation. Results use automated judges (Llama-Guard-3-8B and OpenAI Moderation API). Many step-wise and trajectory results are shown only in figures without exact values.
record.rows_left_out: To stay below 60 rows, omitted Table 1 injection and trajectory-alignment results outside the retained set? None of Table 1 was omitted. Omitted Table 2 non-prefilling attacks and additional attack/benchmark cells; Table 9; most Table 12 ablation cells; Table 3 no-injection outcomes; and supplementary figure-only trajectory results. The retained rows cover all Table 1 models, benchmarks, and judges, plus all Qwen prefilling benchmark/judge cells and the stated benign-injection and post-alignment step findings.

untested.parts: No benign-data fine-tuning. Benign-phrase injections are inference-time interventions.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Decoding-parameter changes are not tested; greedy decoding only.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks.
Does not test whether data or the objective causes shallowness; this is only argued in prose.
Does not measure whether the training spreads the aligned-vs-base difference beyond early tokens (no KL). Fine-tuning attacks against the trained model are not tested.

missing.what: Prefilling Attack column vs no-attack baseline for Qwen (e.g. 1.54→84.81 AdvBench OM) and for Mistral
Mistral prefilling before/after alignment, including the AdvBench OM rise 52.81→77.69 and residual 44.06/63.00
Injection ASR by fixed step (0, 5, 10, 15, 20) on base and aligned Llama
I-GCG suffix ASR before and after alignment on Qwen and Mistral
XSTest over-refusal and MMLU/PROST before and after alignment
Cross-lingual injection results (Korean, Swahili) before and after alignment

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The text says Llama goes 0.00→92.12 (OM), but Table 1 gives no-attack 0.19 OM; the rows correctly use 0.19. Mistral's no-attack ASR is high (19–38%), so its baseline is less safety-aligned than the others. All evaluation uses greedy decoding and automated judges; results differ markedly between the OM and LG judges.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning with a few to a few hundred harmful examples and its effect on refusal.
Fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully chosen benign data. Benign-sounding inference-time injections are not benign fine-tuning.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Decoding changes are not tested. Prefilling and an optimized suffix attack are evaluated in addition to injections at different generation steps.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour; using rank-128 LoRA for training is not a test of localization.
The study proposes trajectory-level training but does not test whether data or an objective causes the original safety shallowness.
Tests trajectory-level training and robustness to injections and attacks; does not measure per-token KL or establish that the training spreads KL-based safety beyond early tokens.
